prompt: A shop's order sheet holds the customer's email on every one of their orders. One of the forty rows has a typo. What is the defect?
hint: Ask what the sheet is able to know, not what a person can see.

choices.text: A spreadsheet is the wrong place to keep an address
choices.why: They are fine there. What is wrong is storing the same one forty times.

choices.text: The typo makes one order undeliverable
choices.why: Costly, but a consequence. The defect is that nothing can tell which copy is wrong.

choices.text: Forty copies take forty times the storage of one
choices.why: Storage is the cheapest thing here and is never the argument.

choices.text: The sheet does not say which copy is right
choices.why: One fact in forty places, and nothing recording that the forty are one person.

prompt: What can a database answer that a spreadsheet cannot?
hint: Think about who decided, and when, that a question would matter.

choices.text: Questions asked by more than one person at once
choices.why: True of a database, but the gap here is about the question, not the asker.

choices.text: Questions that need arithmetic across many rows
choices.why: Spreadsheets are excellent at arithmetic; that was never the gap.

choices.text: Questions about very large amounts of data
choices.why: Size is a real difference and not this one. A small database answers the same questions.

choices.text: Questions nobody planned for
choices.why: A pivot table is a person deciding in advance. A query is not.

prompt: When is a spreadsheet the correct tool and a database the wrong one?
hint: The trade has a price. Ask when the price buys nothing.

choices.text: When there are fewer than a thousand rows
choices.why: Row count decides nothing. A hundred rows two people edit still needs the rules.

choices.text: A database is the better choice here too
choices.why: Three tables to replace four rows is worse, and pretending otherwise is how this gets taught badly.

choices.text: When nobody on the team has written SQL before
choices.why: A reason to learn, not a property of the data.

choices.text: Short-lived data, one writer, no new questions
choices.why: All three of the reasons to pay for the model are absent.

prompt: Complete the one rule the relational model is built on: every fact is written down ___, in one place, and everything that needs it ___ at it.
hint: Two words. The second is what an order does to a customer.

prompt: You ask a database for rows and do not say how to sort them. What are you promised about their order?
hint: A table is a set.

choices.text: The order they were inserted in
choices.why: Common in practice and promised nowhere. It changes as the data grows.

choices.text: Primary key order
choices.why: Often what happens on a small table, which is what makes the habit dangerous.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: A set has no first element, and the order can change over time.

choices.text: The order of the file on disk
choices.why: There is no such order a query is entitled to.

prompt: Which type holds a price?
hint: One of these stores an approximation.

choices.text: real
choices.why: The same approximation with less room.

choices.text: numeric(10,2)
choices.why: Exact decimals. Tenths of a cent survive a thousand additions.

choices.text: text
choices.why: Nothing can be added, compared or summed without converting it first.

choices.text: double precision
choices.why: Binary approximation. The total drifts by cents and nobody notices for a year.

prompt: Customers can be tagged vip, wholesale or newsletter. Why is one boolean column per tag the wrong shape?
hint: Ask what a fourth tag would cost.

choices.text: A fourth tag changes the shape, not the data
choices.why: Data grows in rows; structure grows in columns. A fourth tag means ALTER TABLE and revisiting queries.

choices.text: A boolean column reads more slowly than text does
choices.why: They are not, and speed is not the argument.

choices.text: A boolean column is difficult to index usefully
choices.why: They can. The shape is what is wrong.

choices.text: Three columns is too many for one table
choices.why: Column count is not the problem; what makes a new one necessary is.

prompt: Why is there no order_count column on the customers table?
hint: Ask what would have to happen every time an order is placed.

choices.text: It follows from the orders and would have to be maintained
choices.why: Every insert would have to remember to raise it, and the day one forgets the number is wrong with nothing to check it against.

choices.text: Counting is too slow to store
choices.why: Backwards: storing it is the performance choice, and it is the one with the cost.

choices.text: Updating an integer in place is unreliable
choices.why: They can. The cost is the discipline, not the update.

choices.text: The customers table has no room left for it
choices.why: Tables have no fixed width to fill.

prompt: Two words that decide every shape question: data grows in ___, structure grows in ___.
hint: If adding one more of something means adding the second, the shape is wrong.

prompt: A column declared date refuses the string '03/04/2026'. Why is that refusal worth having?
hint: Think about the column as a whole rather than this one value.

choices.text: Every value is then a date, and comparable
choices.why: Which is what makes sorting and range queries mean something.

choices.text: Dates take less space than text
choices.why: True and irrelevant to why the refusal matters.

choices.text: It forces the application to validate first
choices.why: The point is that it does not have to be trusted to.

choices.text: It stops somebody mistyping a date entirely
choices.why: It prevents one class of them. A wrong but valid date is accepted.

prompt: PRIMARY KEY says two things about a column. Which pair?
hint: One is about other rows; one is about this one.

choices.text: Unique, and never NULL
choices.why: Together: given a value there is exactly one row, or none.

choices.text: Unique, and an integer
choices.why: The type is free. Text and composite keys are both legal.

choices.text: Never NULL, and indexed for speed
choices.why: An index does come with it, and speed is not what the clause promises.

choices.text: Unique, and generated by the database
choices.why: Generation is a separate choice; you may supply the value.

prompt: Why is an email address usually the wrong primary key, even though it is unique?
hint: Unique is only half of what a key needs.

choices.text: An address is too long to repeat across tables
choices.why: Storage is not the cost. The cost is the day somebody updates it.

choices.text: A text key is too slow to index and join on
choices.why: They can, and are, all the time.

choices.text: Two people sometimes share one email address
choices.why: Rare enough not to be the argument. Change is the argument.

choices.text: People change it, and a key has to hold still
choices.why: Stability is the other half, and it is the half the world keeps breaking.

prompt: Where should the uniqueness of an email live, if the primary key is a generated number?
hint: You want both properties, not one instead of the other.

choices.text: In the primary key, as a composite with the id
choices.why: That makes the pair unique, which is no constraint at all on the email.

choices.text: Nowhere — the application checks it
choices.why: Two requests at the same instant both check, both find nothing, and both insert.

choices.text: In a UNIQUE constraint on the email column
choices.why: The row keeps a permanent name and the email keeps its guarantee.

choices.text: In a CHECK constraint
choices.why: A CHECK sees one row and cannot know about the others.

prompt: A customers table holds ids 1, 2, 5 and 6. What does that tell you?
hint: Where does a generated number go when it is not used?

choices.text: Nothing is wrong; rolled-back numbers are gone
choices.why: Gaps are normal, and counting rows by the highest id is what is wrong.

choices.text: The sequence is broken and should be reset
choices.why: It is behaving exactly as designed.

choices.text: Two rows were deleted from the middle of the table
choices.why: Possible, and not something the gap can tell you.

choices.text: Two inserts failed a constraint and should be retried
choices.why: They may have; the table cannot say, and does not need to.

prompt: PRIMARY KEY (flight_id, seat) on a bookings table. What is guaranteed?
hint: Neither column is unique on its own.

choices.text: Each seat number exists once in the table
choices.why: Seat 12A exists on every flight.

choices.text: One booking per seat per flight
choices.why: The combination is what is unique, which is the airline's actual rule.

choices.text: Bookings are stored in flight and seat order
choices.why: Rows have no order, with or without a key.

choices.text: Each flight appears on exactly one booking row
choices.why: flight_id repeats freely; only the pair is constrained.

prompt: Two questions decide any candidate key. Could two different things produce the same value — that asks whether it is ___. Could one thing produce a different value — that asks whether it is ___.
hint: The second word is the one a surrogate key gets for free.

prompt: Match each term to what it names.
hint: Two are about where the value comes from; one is about how many columns.

pairs.right: An identifier that already exists in the world
A value invented by the database that means nothing
Several columns whose combination is unique

right_distractors: A key copied into another table so it can be joined
A column that is unique but may be empty

prompt: What does REFERENCES customers (id) guarantee?
hint: It is about every pointer, forever, not about one insert.

choices.text: Deleting a customer removes the orders they placed
choices.why: Only if you wrote ON DELETE CASCADE, which is a separate decision.

choices.text: Every customer_id names a real customer
choices.why: Referential integrity: not usually, not if the application is careful — always.

choices.text: Orders are fetched together with their customer
choices.why: Fetching is what a query does; this is a rule about what may be stored.

choices.text: The customer's name is copied into the order
choices.why: The opposite: the order holds a number precisely so no copy exists.

prompt: Why is a rule in the database stronger than the same rule in the application?
hint: Count the programs that write to a two-year-old database.

choices.text: More programs write to it than anybody remembers
choices.why: The import, the admin tool, the migration, the fix somebody ran by hand. The rule holds for all of them.

choices.text: The database runs on a more reliable machine
choices.why: Where it runs decides nothing about which rules hold.

choices.text: Databases are written in faster languages
choices.why: Speed is not the property in question.

choices.text: Application code carries more defects per line
choices.why: Not the argument, and not reliably true.

prompt: A customer asks to be deleted and they have three orders. Which ON DELETE belongs on orders.customer_id?
hint: Ask whether an order is a part of the customer or a record of something that happened.

choices.text: RESTRICT — an order is a record of something that happened
choices.why: And the refusal usually reveals you wanted to close the account, not erase the history.

choices.text: CASCADE — the orders belong to that customer and go with them
choices.why: Deleting financial records silently is the expensive version of this mistake.

choices.text: SET NULL — keep the orders, forget the customer
choices.why: Defensible for anonymising, and it needs a nullable column and a deliberate decision.

choices.text: NO ACTION — let the application decide
choices.why: That is the same refusal as RESTRICT, checked later, not a delegation.

prompt: INSERT INTO orders (customer_id) VALUES (77) when no customer 77 exists. What happens?
hint: Think about whether a bad state ever exists.

choices.text: A customer 77 is created automatically to hold it
choices.why: Nothing invents rows.

choices.text: The row is written and flagged for review
choices.why: That is what a report does. A constraint refuses.

choices.text: The statement is refused
choices.why: There is no window during which the bad row exists.

choices.text: The row is written with customer_id set to NULL
choices.why: Nothing silently rewrites your value.

prompt: A shopping basket and its lines. Which ON DELETE on basket_lines.basket_id, and why?
hint: Would anybody ever ask about a basket line whose basket is gone?

choices.text: RESTRICT — a row with children stays until they go
choices.why: A rule of thumb applied without the question behind it, which leaves undeletable baskets.

choices.text: It does not matter, the application deletes both
choices.why: Until the one program that forgets, which is the case the clause exists for.

choices.text: SET NULL — keep the lines for analysis
choices.why: Lines with no basket are rows nobody can interpret.

choices.text: CASCADE — the line is part of the basket
choices.why: The child is a part, not a record. Nobody will ever query it alone.

prompt: Complete the clause that makes an order point at a customer: customer_id integer NOT NULL ___ customers (id).
hint: One word, and it is the name of the whole idea.

prompt: Put the four steps of designing this relationship in the order they happen.
hint: Nothing can point at a table that does not exist yet.
items: Customers gets a primary key that identifies one customer
Orders declares a column to hold a customer's id
That column is declared to REFERENCE customers (id)
An insert naming a customer nobody created is refused
trap: The common swap is declaring the reference before the key exists — a foreign key needs something unique on the far side to point at.

prompt: One customer has many orders. Which table carries the foreign key?
hint: Ask which side can have several of the other.

choices.text: Both tables, so each one can find the other quickly
choices.why: Two copies of one fact, which can then disagree.

choices.text: Neither — a third table holds the pairing
choices.why: That is the shape for many-to-many, and this is not one.

choices.text: orders — one customer per order
choices.why: The key goes on the many side, always.

choices.text: customers, because the customer owns the orders
choices.why: Ownership is not the test; how many is.

prompt: A customers table with a column holding '1001, 1003, 1004'. Which of these problems does that shape cause? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three follow from a list hiding inside a string. One does not.

choices.text: Nothing stops 1003 appearing on a second customer's row
choices.why: The order now has two customers and no rule was broken.

choices.text: Finding the customer for order 1003 means searching text, which also matches 11003
choices.why: This one is caused by it. Searching inside a string has no word boundaries.

choices.text: Two orders placed in the same second can lose one of them
choices.why: Read, append, write back is not safe from two directions at once.

choices.text: Orders can no longer be sorted by date
choices.why: They can — the dates live on the orders and are untouched by this.

prompt: What turns a one-to-many into a one-to-one?
hint: You already have the tool; it is one word.

choices.text: Making the foreign key the primary key of its own table
choices.why: That also works, and it is UNIQUE doing the job, with the surrogate key given up.

choices.text: NOT NULL on the foreign key
choices.why: That makes it mandatory, which is a different decision.

choices.text: A CHECK constraint counting the children
choices.why: A CHECK sees one row and cannot count others.

choices.text: UNIQUE on the foreign key
choices.why: A second child for the same parent is then refused.

prompt: Every employee has exactly one contract. When is it still right to keep contracts in its own table?
hint: Three good reasons, and none of them is tidiness.

choices.text: Because one-to-one relationships always deserve two tables
choices.why: If none of the real reasons applies, one table is simpler and simpler is correct.

choices.text: When salary must be readable by payroll and nobody else
choices.why: Permissions in SQL are granted per table, so splitting is how that rule is expressible.

choices.text: Because a table should not have more than ten columns
choices.why: No such rule exists.

choices.text: Because the contract might later belong to two employees
choices.why: Then it was never one-to-one, and that is a different modelling question.

prompt: The test for which way a relationship goes: ask can this one have several of those in both directions. The side that answers no is where the ___ ___ lives.
hint: Two words, and it is the column that holds the other table's id.

prompt: orders.customer_id is left nullable. What have you decided?
hint: An empty column means something. Say what.

choices.text: That the customer exists but was not written down yet
choices.why: NULL is not a hidden value; it says nobody knows, and the order stands with none.

choices.text: Nullable is the default here, so it says little
choices.why: It is the default and it is still a decision, which is why it is worth making deliberately.

choices.text: That the foreign key is no longer enforced
choices.why: It is enforced for every non-null value; only the absence is permitted.

choices.text: That an order is allowed to have no customer
choices.why: Which is right for a shop where anybody may buy without an account, and wrong for one that requires signing in.

prompt: An order contains several products and a product is on several orders. What does the model require?
hint: Neither side is the one.

choices.text: Two foreign keys, one on each table
choices.why: Two copies of one fact, free to disagree.

choices.text: A foreign key on whichever table is larger
choices.why: There is no larger side; both answer several.

choices.text: A list column on orders naming the products
choices.why: A list inside a column is the shape this replaces.

choices.text: A third table holding both foreign keys
choices.why: Every many-to-many in every relational database that has existed is a third table.

prompt: PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id) on order_lines. What does adding another kettle to order 1002 do?
hint: A second row for the same pair is refused.

choices.text: A second row is inserted for the same pair
choices.why: Refused by the primary key.

choices.text: The order is rejected as a duplicate
choices.why: The order is untouched; only a second identical line would be refused.

choices.text: The quantity on the existing row goes up
choices.why: Which is the rule the composite key expresses: one line per product per order.

choices.text: A new order is created
choices.why: Nothing creates orders on its own.

prompt: unit_price sits on order_lines while price sits on products. Why is that not the duplication this model forbids?
hint: Are they the same fact?

choices.text: The line is a copy kept for speed
choices.why: That would be denormalisation, which is a performance decision. This is not one.

choices.text: Prices are too small to worry about duplicating
choices.why: Size never decides this.

choices.text: The product price is a suggestion the line may override
choices.why: It is the current price and it is authoritative — for today, which is the point.

choices.text: Two different facts, equal once
choices.why: What this costs and what this cost that day are independent, and independent facts are stored independently.

prompt: If unit_price were NOT stored on the line and were read from products instead, what breaks?
hint: Think about an invoice printed last month.

choices.text: Products can no longer be discontinued
choices.why: Unrelated, and handled by a flag rather than a price.

choices.text: The primary key of order_lines stops being unique
choices.why: The key is the two ids and is untouched.

choices.text: Orders can no longer be joined to products
choices.why: The join is unaffected; only what it reports changes.

choices.text: Past orders re-price themselves
choices.why: The March invoice stops matching the database in April, and nothing went wrong that anybody can point at.

prompt: Why do the two ON DELETE clauses on order_lines disagree with each other?
hint: One side is a part; the other is a record.

choices.text: It is a mistake and both should be CASCADE
choices.why: Both as CASCADE would delete sales history when a product is removed.

choices.text: A table is permitted a single CASCADE clause
choices.why: No such rule.

choices.text: One side holds parts, the other holds history
choices.why: The two sides of a join table are usually not symmetrical, even though it looks like it treats them the same.

choices.text: Products are referenced more often, so they need protecting
choices.why: Frequency is not the criterion; meaning is.

prompt: A table whose primary key is two foreign keys is not a thing; it is a ___. The name for it is a ___ table.
hint: The second word is what you would call the table that sits in the middle.

prompt: Match each column of order_lines to what it belongs to.
hint: One of these is true of the pairing rather than of either end.

pairs.right: Which order this line is part of
A fact about this product on this order, and nowhere else

right_distractors: How many of this product exist in the warehouse
How many orders this product has appeared on

prompt: What does NULL mean?
hint: It is not a value at all.

choices.text: Unknown — nobody recorded it
choices.why: Which is why comparing it to anything gives unknown.

choices.text: Zero, written a shorter way
choices.why: Zero is a number and a perfectly good answer. Storing it as NULL throws away a fact.

choices.text: A column absent from this table
choices.why: The column exists; it is this row's value that is absent.

choices.text: An empty string
choices.why: The empty string is a value, and a strange one, but it is known.

prompt: SELECT NULL = NULL returns what?
hint: Can anybody answer a question about two things they do not know?

choices.text: NULL
choices.why: Is this unknown the same as that unknown? Nobody can say.

choices.text: true
choices.why: The intuition everybody has, and it is the source of most NULL bugs.

choices.text: An error
choices.why: It is a perfectly valid expression, which is what makes it dangerous.

choices.text: false
choices.why: Not false either — SQL has a third truth value for exactly this.

prompt: Ten customers, three with city NULL. WHERE city = 'Porto' gives 4 and WHERE city <> 'Porto' gives 3. Where are the other three?
hint: WHERE keeps rows where the condition is true.

choices.text: In the second, because they are not Porto
choices.why: Nobody knows whether they are Porto, so the condition is unknown rather than true.

choices.text: In neither, since unknown is not true
choices.why: Both queries are correct; the arithmetic you did in your head was not.

choices.text: In both answers, so the total counts them twice
choices.why: Nothing is counted twice; they are counted zero times.

choices.text: Excluded by the database as invalid rows
choices.why: They are perfectly valid rows with one unknown column.

prompt: SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) returns how many rows?
hint: Unfold the NOT IN into a chain of ANDs.

choices.text: Rows outside the list, since NULL matches no value
choices.why: It matches nothing and poisons the chain.

choices.text: Zero, always, whatever the table holds
choices.why: id <> NULL is unknown, so the whole AND can never be true — and no error is reported.

choices.text: The rows other than 1 and 2
choices.why: The intuition, and the NULL destroys it silently.

choices.text: An error, because NULL is in the list
choices.why: No error. That is precisely the danger.

prompt: A UNIQUE column accepts three rows all holding NULL. Why?
hint: Uniqueness is about values being equal.

choices.text: Nobody knows two unknowns are equal, so nothing collides
choices.why: Correct by the logic, and surprising the first time. UNIQUE is not the tool for at most one empty.

choices.text: The constraint was declared wrongly
choices.why: It behaves exactly as the standard says.

choices.text: The first NULL is stored and the rest are discarded
choices.why: All three rows exist.

choices.text: UNIQUE applies to text that has something in it
choices.why: It applies to values; NULL is not one.

prompt: The values are 10, 20 and NULL. What does avg() return?
hint: Which rows does an aggregate count?

choices.why: Aggregates ignore nulls, so the average is over the two known values.
That would be treating the unknown as a zero, which is exactly what NULL is not.

choices.text: An error, because one value is unknown
choices.why: It is skipped rather than refused.

choices.text: NULL
choices.why: Aggregates do not propagate it the way arithmetic does.

prompt: Comparing with `=` never works on an unknown. Write the two-word operator that asks whether a column holds no value: ___ ___.
hint: Two words, and together they are the only way to find the empty rows.

prompt: A quantity that is zero. Should the column hold NULL?
hint: Is the fact missing, or is the fact zero?

choices.text: Yes, so the row can be filtered out easily
choices.why: Filtering is easier on a real zero, and NULL makes every later query need two conditions.

choices.text: Yes — zero and empty mean the same thing
choices.why: They do not. One is known and one is not.

choices.text: Yes, if the column is also declared UNIQUE
choices.why: Unrelated to what the value means.

choices.text: No — zero is a fact you have
choices.why: Storing it as unknown throws away a fact you had.

prompt: CHECK (ends_on > starts_on) on a row where ends_on is NULL. Is the row accepted?
hint: A CHECK refuses on false, and unknown is not false.

choices.text: Yes — unknown is not false
choices.why: A CHECK on a nullable column is not the rule you think you wrote.

choices.text: No — CHECK requires both columns to be NOT NULL
choices.why: It has no such requirement.

choices.text: Yes, and the database logs a warning
choices.why: Nothing is logged. The row is simply accepted.

choices.text: No — the comparison fails and the row is refused
choices.why: It fails none of them; it makes them unknown.

prompt: Which rule cannot be written as a CHECK?
hint: A CHECK sees one row.

choices.text: The price is zero or above
choices.why: One column of one row, the simplest case.

choices.text: At most three bookings per customer
choices.why: Answering it means counting rows elsewhere, which a CHECK may not do.

choices.text: The end date is after the start date
choices.why: Two columns of the same row is allowed and useful.

choices.text: The status is one of four permitted words
choices.why: A list membership test on this row's value.

prompt: The application checks that an email is unique before inserting. Why is that not enough?
hint: Two requests arrive at the same moment.

choices.text: Selecting before inserting is too slow
choices.why: Speed is not the flaw; the gap between the two statements is.

choices.text: The application might have a bug in the check
choices.why: True of any code and not the specific reason this approach cannot work.

choices.text: Both find nothing and both insert
choices.why: A UNIQUE constraint cannot be beaten this way: the check and the write are one operation inside the database.

choices.text: Emails differ in case and the check misses that
choices.why: A real issue and a different one.

prompt: Product categories that somebody non-technical will want to add. CHECK, ENUM or a table?
hint: The giveaway is who adds a value, and whether the value needs properties.

choices.text: An ENUM type
choices.why: Reusable across tables, and altering it is vendor-specific and awkward.

choices.text: A table with a foreign key
choices.why: A new category is one INSERT, and the category can carry a label, an order, a colour.

choices.text: CHECK (category IN (…))
choices.why: Right for a fixed list that is part of the design, and this is not one.

choices.text: A plain text column with no constraint
choices.why: The one answer that is never right: it ends up holding four spellings of the same word.

prompt: Which of these is a cost of constraints, stated honestly?
hint: Three of these are made up; one is real and worth knowing.

choices.text: Removing one after it is added is not supported
choices.why: They can, and relaxing one on a table that obeyed it is easy.

choices.text: They prevent the use of transactions
choices.why: Unrelated; constraints are checked inside transactions.

choices.text: They slow a query down when it reads back
choices.why: They cost on write, not on read.

choices.text: Bulk loading is always slower, row by row
choices.why: Which is why the answer is to load, then add them, validating the whole table once.

prompt: Name the constraint for each job. Refuses a second row with the same value: ___. Refuses an empty value: ___ ___.
hint: Three words in total, and all three are SQL keywords.

prompt: Reading an unfamiliar schema, you find a table whose primary key is two foreign keys. What have you found?
hint: It is not a thing.

choices.text: A table with no rows of its own
choices.why: It has rows; each one is a pairing.

choices.text: A table that was designed badly
choices.why: It is the correct and only shape for many-to-many.

choices.text: A view presented as though it were a table
choices.why: A view is a different object entirely.

choices.text: A relationship, not a thing
choices.why: Spotting them immediately tells you which pairs are many-to-many.

prompt: In psql's \d output, which section answers who points at this table?
hint: The CREATE TABLE cannot answer it, which is why this exists.

choices.text: Indexes
choices.why: What is indexed, which is a different question.

choices.text: Check constraints
choices.why: Rules about this table's own rows.

choices.text: Foreign-key constraints
choices.why: That is the other direction: who this table points at.

choices.text: Referenced by
choices.why: The part people miss, and what you need before changing or deleting anything.

prompt: Reading a schema you inherited, which of these is a defect worth asking about?
hint: One of these is a rule that was never written down.

choices.text: A generated integer key on each of the tables
choices.why: That is the recommended default.

choices.text: A nullable city column on customers
choices.why: Defensible, as long as somebody can say what an empty one means.

choices.text: A join table with a composite primary key
choices.why: The correct shape for many-to-many.

choices.text: A money column typed as double precision, which drifts
choices.why: The total drifts by cents over a thousand rows, and it is the most expensive type mistake there is.

prompt: Put the seven steps of modelling something new in order.
hint: You cannot decide what belongs to a pairing before you know there is one.
items: Name the things, one table each, with a surrogate key
Write the facts about each thing as typed columns
Ask several? in both directions for every relationship
Put what belongs to a pairing into the join table
Make every column NOT NULL unless you can describe the empty one
Decide each ON DELETE by part or record
Add a CHECK wherever you would write a comment
trap: The common swap is deciding nullability before the relationships exist — a foreign key you have not created yet cannot be made mandatory.

prompt: A library keeps one table called `member_loans`, holding the member's name, the member's email, the book's title and the day it went out. Which test does that table fail?
hint: Try saying out loud what one row of it is.

choices.text: Its columns are in an order nobody agreed on
choices.why: Columns have no order that matters, any more than rows do.

choices.text: "Each row is one ______" cannot be finished with one noun
choices.why: A row is a member and a loan at once, so nothing in it is the member for anything else to point at.

choices.text: It declares no primary key
choices.why: It may well declare one. That would not mend a table holding two kinds of thing.

choices.text: A title is text where it should be a number
choices.why: A title is a fine fact about a book. What is wrong is that the book is not a row anywhere.

prompt: The library is split into `members`, `books` and `loans`. A member borrows many books over the years, and a copy of a book is lent to many members. Where do the foreign keys go?
hint: Ask "can this one have several of those?" in both directions.

choices.text: `book_id` on `members` and `member_id` on `books`
choices.why: A column holds one value, and each of those sides has many.

choices.text: `member_id` on `books`, since a book is out to one person at a time
choices.why: That records the loan happening now and forgets every loan before it.

choices.text: Both on `loans`, which is the relationship and carries the dates
choices.why: Both directions answer yes, so the pairing is a thing, and the dates are facts about the pairing.

choices.text: `member_id` on `loans`; the book is found by matching its title
choices.why: Joining on a title is the copied fact this whole lesson is against.

prompt: A school has `students`, `courses` and `enrolments`, and every enrolment ends in a grade. Which table does `grade` belong on?
hint: Ask which noun the number is about.

choices.text: `students`, because the grade is the student's
choices.why: A student has one grade per course, and a column holds one value.

choices.text: `courses`, because the course awards it
choices.why: A course awards many of them, one per student.

choices.text: Either end will do; it is one number
choices.why: It belongs to neither end. It is true of the pairing and of nothing else.

choices.text: `enrolments`, because it is a fact about one student in one course
choices.why: That is the test for a column on a join table, and the reason `unit_price` sits on the line.

prompt: A new invoicing system needs a column for the amount due. Which type, and why?
hint: One of these is the mistake this lesson calls the most expensive in a table.

choices.text: `double precision`, which is fast and has plenty of range
choices.why: It stores approximations. Add a thousand invoices and the total is out by a few cents.

choices.text: `numeric(10,2)`, which stores the decimal exactly
choices.why: Money goes here. The value that comes back is the value that went in.

choices.text: `real`, since two decimal places need very little precision
choices.why: The count of decimals is not the problem. Binary cannot represent a tenth at all.

choices.text: `text`, so the amount reads back exactly as it was typed
choices.why: Then nothing can add two of them, and sorting puts 100 before 99.

prompt: A `deliveries` table has `delivered_on date` and no `NOT NULL`. A weekly report counts the rows `WHERE delivered_on <> current_date`. What does it leave out every week, without ever failing?
hint: Add up what the two opposite conditions return.

choices.text: Nothing; `<>` is the opposite of `=`
choices.why: It is, for values. An unknown is a value in neither answer.

choices.text: Only the deliveries made today
choices.why: Those are the ones it means to leave out.

choices.text: Every delivery that has not happened yet
choices.why: Their date is unknown, so the comparison is unknown, and `WHERE` keeps only what is true.

choices.text: Every delivery older than a week
choices.why: Nothing in that condition mentions how old a row is.

prompt: `invoice_lines` references `invoices`, and `invoices` references `currencies`. Which `ON DELETE` belongs on each?
hint: For each child, ask whether it is a part or a record of something that occurred.

choices.text: `CASCADE` on both
choices.why: Deleting a currency would then delete every invoice ever issued in it.

choices.text: `RESTRICT` on both
choices.why: An invoice could then never be deleted until somebody removed its lines by hand.

choices.text: `CASCADE` on the line's invoice, `RESTRICT` on the invoice's currency
choices.why: A line means nothing without its invoice; an invoice is a record, and its currency cannot be un-chosen.

choices.text: `SET NULL` on both, so nothing is ever lost
choices.why: A line with no invoice and an invoice with no currency are rows that say nothing.

prompt: A colleague proposes `email` as the primary key of `customers`, since it is unique anyway. Which is the argument against it?
hint: Two questions decide a candidate key. It passes one of them.

choices.text: An email is too long to be efficient as a key
choices.why: Length is a performance detail, and it is not the objection.

choices.text: Two customers might share an address
choices.why: They might, and a `UNIQUE` column already forbids it. The problem is the other question.

choices.text: Most databases will not accept text as a primary key
choices.why: They will. Nothing about the type is the objection.

choices.text: A key must never change, and an address changes
choices.why: It is unique and it is not stable, and a key needs both.

prompt: A blog's `posts` table has a `tags text` column holding `'sql, databases'`. Somebody asks how many posts are tagged `sql`. Why is that hard to answer correctly?
hint: Say what the search would actually have to look for.

choices.text: Searching for text inside text matches `nosql` as well
choices.why: It is a list hiding in a string, and the search cannot tell where one tag ends.

choices.text: The posts have no primary key to count by
choices.why: They may have one. The tags would still be a list in a string.

choices.text: The column should be `varchar` rather than `text`
choices.why: In PostgreSQL that changes nothing whatever.

choices.text: Tags come back in no order, so a count is unreliable
choices.why: No count depends on an order, and rows have none anyway.

prompt: A `bookings` table declares `UNIQUE (room_id, starts_at)` and leaves `room_id` nullable. Two rows arrive with an empty `room_id` and the same `starts_at`. What does the database do?
hint: Ask what comparing two unknowns answers.

choices.text: Refuses the second, since the pair repeats
choices.why: The pair repeats only if the empty halves are equal, and nothing knows that they are.

choices.text: Refuses the second, because a `UNIQUE` column may not be empty
choices.why: That is `NOT NULL`. `UNIQUE` says nothing about emptiness.

choices.text: Accepts both, and warns about the repeated time
choices.why: There is no warning. It is an ordinary insert breaking no rule.

choices.text: Accepts both, because two unknowns are not known to be equal
choices.why: The same reason a `UNIQUE` column takes any number of empty rows.

prompt: A `deliveries` table holds 60 rows. `WHERE delivered_on = '2026-03-02'` counts 12 of them, and `WHERE delivered_on <> '2026-03-02'` counts 40. Write how many rows are in neither count.
hint: The two opposite conditions do not have to add up.

prompt: You are handed a schema you have never seen. Put the five passes over it in the order that gets you oriented fastest.
hint: Each pass answers a question the next one needs.
items: Say out loud what one row of each table is
Find the tables whose primary key is two foreign keys
Read the NOT NULLs as what this system requires
Read the ON DELETEs as what this system treats as disposable
Look for the constraints that are not there
trap: The common swap is hunting for missing constraints first — you cannot say what is missing from a table until you know what the table is.

prompt: A school with `students`, `courses` and `enrolments`. Match each column to what it is a fact about.
hint: One of the three belongs to neither end of the relationship.
